doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Closing wish: people should dance to the music again
summary: Rowe thanks him; Grosz says dance gigs were the best he ever had and laments jazz becoming showy concert music.

story.theme_name: Thanks and goodbyes: closing the interview
story.community_name: Closing thanks and goodbyes at the end of the interview

blocks.x: We have really enjoyed talking with you today. And on behalf of Hamilton College I’d like to thank Marty Grosz for joining us. You have a unique perspective on, in fact, it’s reflected in what you do. You know you’re one of the few guys who plays acoustically.

No I don’t look upon it as anything else, if I can just do one thing, I look upon it as an entertainment. And I wish to make one closing statement, I wish that people would dance to the music again. The best jobs I ever had in my life were dance gigs. And I don’t mean that because it’s a lost thing and nobody’s doing it anymore and so I hark back to it, but I mean they were really fun because you could really play unselfconsciously. Just as long as they didn’t pay any attention to you, you served a purpose, you got them on the floor, and got them milling about and everything like that and jumping to the music, and that was when I heard piano players and stuff play so freely and so strangely, and so inspiredly, because they didn’t have to rely upon, you know, hitting home runs, which you know jazz has become concert stage music. And guys hit home runs. They play high notes, they do drum solos that go on forever and ever and ever, and these sure-fire devices just like concert artists do with their cadenzas and their bravura performances and stuff. And that didn’t used to be. You used to play in little joints and saloons or in little dance places and just play unselfconsciously. And that was the most fun of all. And if you could have a few laughs doing, entertain a little bit, great. And if the music happened to work as well and be good, that I always felt was a bonus. You know the first thing was

just to hear the melody and have a good beat. And then if it got going, and if somebody really started improvising, but it was done without a thought to I gotta get ‘em—I gotta kill ‘em. You know, this guy took three choruses, I got to take four choruses ‘cause I gotta top him. It wasn’t that kind of feel. You know just keep the thing going and play something interesting.
